prompt.context: John Malone of TCI commissions you to look into a concern that he has. He has heard that Hughes is planning to launch a commercial satellite that will offer cable TV services to the domestic market.
prompt.question: Is this a credible threat to John's monopoly position in cable TV services? If it is credible, what should TCI do?

clarifying_info.q: How much would it cost Hughes to get the satellite operational?
clarifying_info.a: $5 billion upfront investment to get the satellite in the air and operational.

clarifying_info.q: What channel offerings would the satellite provide compared to TCI?
clarifying_info.a: Hughes would offer 200 channels; TCI currently offers only 50 channels.

clarifying_info.q: How long would the satellite last?
clarifying_info.a: Satellites generally last 7-10 years, but due to rapid technology evolution the practical useful life of this satellite is 5 years.

clarifying_info.q: How many customers does TCI currently have?
clarifying_info.a: TCI has 40 million customers across the country.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average current cable bill?
clarifying_info.a: On average, current cable bills are $35 per month.

framework: Assess credibility of the threat: estimate Hughes's revenue potential and cost structure to determine if the business is viable
Revenue side: estimate addressable market (number of households willing to pay) and price point Hughes must charge to compete

Cost side: amortize the $5B upfront satellite investment over useful life (5 years), plus fixed operating costs (sales, service, programming rights) and variable costs (satellite dish per customer — or lease model)
Compare revenue vs. total costs to judge viability and threat credibility
If threat is credible, generate strategic responses for TCI

questions.prompt: Estimate the price Hughes would need to charge to be a competitive threat.
questions.guidance: Hughes must price close to TCI's current $35/month average bill. It could justify a slight premium given 200 vs. 50 channels, but must remain broadly competitive. Establish ~$35/month as the anchor price for the analysis.

questions.prompt: Estimate the number of potential satellite TV customers Hughes could capture.
questions.guidance: Start with 100M US households. Approximately 60% are in the market for cable services (combination of income levels and need for reception, which varies by region) — giving 60M cable-eligible households. TCI has 40M customers. Assume Hughes could realistically penetrate 50% of TCI's existing base, yielding 20M potential satellite subscribers.

math.setup: Total US households = 100M; cable-eligible = 60% × 100M = 60M; TCI customers = 40M; Hughes penetration assumption = 50% of TCI base

questions.prompt: Amortize the $5B satellite investment over its useful life to find the annual capital charge per customer.
questions.guidance: The satellite has a practical useful life of 5 years (not the physical 7-10 years, because technology evolves quickly). Dividing $5B by 5 years gives $1B/year that must be recovered. With 20M customers that is $50/customer/year or roughly $4.17/month.

math.setup: Initial cost = $5B; useful life = 5 years; assumed customer base = 20M

questions.prompt: Assess whether Hughes's total cost structure allows it to profitably serve customers at ~$35/month.
questions.guidance: Fixed costs: with 20M customers the amortization is $50/year per customer. Add costs of sales, service, and acquiring programming rights. Variable costs: the satellite dish for each consumer is a large upfront cost — but if Hughes leases dishes (rolled into the monthly bill, similar to how cable boxes are leased today), this one-time burden is spread out. The combined operating costs under the dish-leasing model come in low enough that the service can be priced around $35/month while remaining economically viable, making the threat credible.

math.setup: Revenue per customer: ~$35/month = $420/year; annual capital charge: $50/year; remaining margin for fixed ops + dish lease: $420 - $50 = $370/year per customer
steps: Remaining to cover operations and dish lease: $420 - $50 = $370
Conclusion: sufficient margin exists to cover sales, service, programming, and dish leasing costs — threat is economically viable
math.answer: Hughes can viably serve customers at ~$35/month; the threat is credible

questions.prompt: Given the threat is credible, what strategic options does TCI have?
questions.guidance: A strong answer covers multiple response vectors: offensive (match or exceed satellite offering), defensive (lock competitors out), and M&A. Candidate should structure 3-4 clear options with brief rationale for each.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic responses should TCI (John Malone) pursue in response to Hughes's satellite TV threat?

categories.name: Compete directly
ideas: Launch TCI's own satellite TV service to match or exceed Hughes's 200-channel offering
Partner with an existing satellite operator to accelerate time to market

categories.name: Acquire or neutralize
ideas: Buy out Hughes's satellite TV initiative before it launches
Invest in or acquire Hughes to control the threat

categories.name: Improve existing product
ideas: Rapidly expand TCI's channel lineup to close the 200 vs. 50 channel gap
Invest in infrastructure upgrades (e.g., fiber, digital cable) to improve quality and breadth

categories.name: Lock out competition
ideas: Negotiate exclusive content agreements with key programmers to prevent Hughes from acquiring must-have channels
Secure long-term subscriber contracts with loyalty incentives or early-termination fees

categories.name: Pricing and bundling
ideas: Bundle cable with broadband internet and phone (triple play) to raise switching costs
Offer promotional pricing to retain at-risk subscribers in regions most vulnerable to satellite competition

recommendation: The Hughes satellite TV threat is credible: the economics work at a ~$35/month price point under a dish-leasing model, and the 200-channel offering significantly outpaces TCI's 50 channels

TCI should pursue a multi-pronged response: (1) develop or acquire its own satellite capability, and (2) aggressively expand channel offerings while securing exclusive programming deals to raise barriers to entry
risks: Satellite launch delays or technical failures could change the competitive timeline
If TCI over-invests in exclusive content, programming costs could compress margins
A price war could erode profitability for both TCI and Hughes
next_steps: Commission a rapid feasibility study on acquiring Hughes's satellite initiative or launching TCI's own
Open negotiations with top-tier content providers for exclusive or preferential distribution rights
Model triple-play bundling economics (cable + broadband + phone) to increase customer stickiness before Hughes launches
